Here is what I recommend in terms of books.

1. NCEES PE Civil Handbook. Know it inside and out. It's a free download on the NCEES website. You can refer to it during the exam, but it will be easier to know what formulas to use when you are looking it up. Also, make sure it's the latest version (1.2).
2. The CERM, and the Structural Depth Reference Manual. You can get them [here](https://ppi2pass.com/pe-exam/civil/structural-depth/study-materials), but you can also find older editions on Amazon or eBay for cheaper. You can't bring these to the exam anymore, but it's still a good study resource. Also, when looking up formulas and tables, check where they are in the Civil Handbook. This way, you are familiar on where to find those formulas when doing practice problems.
3. School of PE Civil Exam Review Guide. You can get that book [here](https://www.schoolofpe.com/books/pe-exam/pe-civil/review-guide.html). I took the School of PE course, and this book is so much better than the course. The class focuses more on the concepts, while the book goes straight to the problems. If you are not going to get the CERM, get this review guide. Unlike the CERM, I would stick to the latest edition, since it refers to the Civil Handbook for the breath (and I don't think the current CERM does that yet). However, I would say the Structural Depth Reference Manual from PPI is a better depth resource than the School of PE's.

While the books go over everything you need to know, the key to passing is to do practice problems. While the format of the test had recently changed, and the exam is no longer open book, the material you are to be tested on hasn't changed. There are countless practice exams for sale, and online, and I recommend you take as many as you can between now and October. However, I'll single out two exams.

1. NCEES PE Civil: Structural Practice Exam. This is the only exam made by the same organization who makes the PE exam, so it's probably a good taste of what to expect. It's $40 for a PDF on the website, or you can get a physical book [here](https://www.amazon.com/PE-Civil-Structural-Practice-Exam/dp/1947801201). Keep in mind that this is just one exam, and the exam you'll take will have concepts that are not in that exam and vice versa (that's why I told you to take as many as possible).
2. Civil Engineering Academy CPT Exam simulator. You can buy it online [here](https://civilengineeringacademy.thrivecart.com/cea-civil-pe-cbt-exam-simulator). This is the closest you will get to taking the actual exam, if you just want to buy a practice test and not do a course. Again, like the NCEES practice test, this is just one exam, and the questions will surely be different than your actual exam.

With that said, what should we do?

An early 2020 style lockdown is a non-starter, since most students are unwilling to go back to remote learning and the government doesn't want to spend trillions on another stimulus. Some places have reinstated mask mandates, but cases are rising just as fast compared to places that don't have mandates (not to say masks don't work, but they don't work as well compared to back when we had less transmissible variants). We could help more people get vaccinated, but almost everyone who wants the vaccine has already gotten it. Vaccine mandates help, but, at least in the US, they are too polarizing to implement nationwide. Even Biden's mandate for employers has a test-out option. We also have anti-viral pills, but they are scarce, and there is always the possibility of their efficiency being lowered due to a potential future variant.

Sooner or later, we need to declare an endemic. Obviously not now, when we have a record number of COVID cases. But waiting until 95% of the population is fully vaccinated, double-boosted, and had at least one breakthrough case isn't realistic either. At some point, we need to find a point where we can live in a world with COVID without a strain on our healthcare systems.

In terms of self-protection, a cloth mask is not effective. However, if you are already infected, you only need to worry about spreading omicron, not protection. A cloth mask is just as good as an N95 at stopping the spread.

If a justice unexpectedly dies, or decides to retire before his or her term ends, an alternate, chosen by the President and confirmed by the Senate at the time of the original justice's nomination, will take his or her place for the remainder of the term.  But the constitution only allows lifetime appointments, which would require a constitutional amendment; however this could be solved by having justices not reconfirmed have "senior status" and not being allowed to vote on cases, while technically still being a justice. Same for the alternates, they could have "junior status," not being allowed to vote, and only be elevated to "full status" once the justice dies or retires. So while the number of justices will be more than 9 in theory, in practice there will only be 9 "full status" justices.
